title: The Jacket That Freed Lindy Chamberlain
central_question: How did a mother convicted of murdering her baby come to be cleared, and what was the 'blood' in her car?
content_notes: Non-graphic. No depiction of the child, of violence, or of blood. All scenes are labelled illustrations; no real photographs, documents or footage are imitated.

lines.text: A mother was jailed for life for murdering her baby.
But the 'baby's blood' in her car was never blood.
August 1980. A campsite at Uluru.
Lindy Chamberlain said a dingo took her nine week old daughter, Azaria, from their tent.
Azaria was never found. Her jumpsuit was, near the rock.
But not the matinee jacket Lindy said Azaria wore over it.
Prosecutors said she killed Azaria in the family car,
and that tests found a baby's blood. Even a spray of it, under the dashboard.
October 1982: guilty of murder. Life, with hard labour.
In 1984, the High Court rejected her appeal, three votes to two.
Then, in early 1986, a tourist fell to his death from Uluru.
Searching near dingo dens below the rock, police found something else.
Azaria's matinee jacket.
Five days later, Lindy was released from prison.
Then a Royal Commission re-examined the science.
The 'blood spray' under the dashboard? Sound-deadening compound, applied at the factory.
No blood was found in the car at all.
In 1988, all the convictions were quashed.
But only in 2012 did a coroner finally rule how Azaria died:
attacked and taken by a dingo.
Just as her mother said, almost thirty-two years earlier.

claims.text: Azaria disappeared on 17 August 1980 from the family's tent at the Uluru (Ayers Rock) campsite, Northern Territory.
Lindy Chamberlain said a dingo had taken nine-week-old Azaria from the tent.
Azaria's body was never found; her jumpsuit was found near the base of the rock about a week later.
The matinee jacket Lindy said Azaria wore over the jumpsuit was not found with it.
The prosecution case was that Lindy killed Azaria in the family car.
Forensic evidence at trial alleged infant (foetal) blood in the car, including a 'spray' under the dashboard.
On 29 October 1982 Lindy was convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment with hard labour.
Michael Chamberlain was convicted as an accessory after the fact (18-month suspended sentence).
The High Court dismissed the appeal 3-2 on 22 February 1984 (Chamberlain v R (No 2) [1984] HCA 7).

In early 1986 a British tourist fell to his death from Uluru; searchers looked for his remains below the rock, in an area of dingo lairs. (Exact date of the fall varies by source; not named on screen.)
Azaria's matinee jacket was found on 2 February 1986, partly buried near a dingo lair, during that search.
Lindy was released on 7 February 1986 (sentence remitted; not a pardon), five days after the jacket was found.
A Royal Commission (Justice Trevor Morling) re-examined the evidence; its 1987 report found serious doubts about the convictions.
The 'spray' under the dashboard was a sound-deadening compound applied by the manufacturer; the inquiry found no blood in the car.
On 15 September 1988 the NT Court of Criminal Appeal quashed all convictions of Lindy and Michael Chamberlain.
On 12 June 2012, at the fourth inquest, NT Coroner Elizabeth Morris found Azaria's death was caused by being 'attacked and taken by a dingo'.
